summary: This RFC defines a way for the two ends of a Telnet connection to exchange the type of terminal being used. That lets a host treat a user's screen correctly. It was replaced by RFC 930.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 884 defines a Telnet option for reporting the terminal type to a server. The server can request the name, and the client can return it in the connection.

subtitle: A Telnet option lets a client report its terminal type to a server.

tldr.problem: A Telnet server may need to know which terminal is connected so a process can adapt output to that terminal's characteristics.
tldr.mechanism: The TERMINAL-TYPE option lets the server request a terminal name and the client return it as an NVT ASCII string.
tldr.outcome: The option provides a way to exchange terminal type information, and RFC 884 was later obsoleted by RFC 930.

today: RFC 884 was obsoleted by RFC 930. It documents an earlier version of the Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option.

sections.title: The Terminal-Type Option
sections.content: RFC 884 defines the Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option with code 24. It allows a server to determine the type of terminal connected to a user Telnet program. The RFC notes that the information may be passed to a process that can adapt data to the terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can learn the kind of terminal connected to the client. A process may use that information to tailor its output.

sections.title: Requesting and Sending a Terminal Name
sections.content: The two sides use WILL and DO to grant permission to exchange terminal type information. The sender of DO may request the type with a SEND subcommand. The sender of WILL transmits the name in an IS subcommand as an NVT ASCII string; uppercase and lowercase are equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can ask for a terminal name, and the client can reply with it. The name is sent as text, and letter case does not matter.

sections.title: Terminal Names and Alternatives
sections.content: The RFC lists example terminal names for IBM, TOPS-20, and Unix environments and points to the Assigned Numbers RFC for the complete list. A client may answer successive SEND requests with names from most specific to more generic. If the type is unknown or unlikely to be recognized, the RFC says to use “UNKNOWN.”
sections.plainLanguage: A terminal may have a specific name and a more general one. The client can offer alternatives if the server does not recognize the first name.
